In reply to the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) about arrangements for the return to the lake ships of crews recently on strike, I will outline the instructions given in this connection covering both those who previously manned the ships and new men the companies might require.
The order issued by the government requires every unlicensed man, that is a man below officer rank, who was a member of the crew of a boat at the time of the stoppage of work quoted, to return to his boat and duties. If the master of the ship finds it necessary to increase his crew he is required to obtain men from the nearest national employment office. If and when an employment office obtains a request for men from the master of a ship the staff shall follow the normal procedure, and in respect to union membership that procedure is to check to see if the shipping company has an agreement with the union and to comply with the terms of the agreement. If, for example, as is the case with some of the companies, the agreement requires that only members of a certain organization shall be employed, it is the duty of the employment office to assist in seeing that the agreement is carried out. This is customary practice and one which is well understood by our officials and others concerned.

Mr. Speaker, certain remarks were made last evening by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) which I feel should not be permitted to pass without being elaborated upon or explained and the other side of the picture presented to this house. I regret there was not time to do this last evening, when we were all in the mood to continue the discussion. The hon. member for Rosthern mentioned that if we were going to discuss all the details of veterans affairs upon which agreement had not been reached in the veterans affairs committee, we might be here until next September; in fact he suggested that the whole time of this house might be taken up with veterans affairs
Soldier Settlement

from now until September. I should like to point out that the house has had very few opportunities during this session to discuss the affairs of the returned men and women. Many of us on both sides are here because at the time of the last election we were interested in trying to do something for our comrades, and I am quite certain that was the main motive which prompted many new members to seek election. I do not think I am exaggerating if I say that the reestablishment of our ex-service men and women, both of this war and of world war I, is one of the main issues of the day. I pine for the cool breezes of the Pacific coast and I am anxious to get home, just as are the majority of members here. But if it is necessary for us to stay here until next September in order that we may get well-deserved benefits for old soldiers, what of it?
Why September? We will go to Christmas. I am willing to go to Christmas. I am here to stay, to the last shot.

If that is the only interruption to-day, I shall not mind.
Reference was made to the method of conducting the business in the committee of veterans affairs. I wish to have the record straight in this respect. While the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) gave his impressions and his interpretation of how the business of that committee is being conducted, I do not think all members see that business being conducted in quite the same way as he did.
I hold in my hand an article written by Mr. Walter A. Tucker, the chairman of the parliamentary committee-who, of course, is the hon. member for Rosthern-published in Veterans Affairs, which is a publication under the authority of the Hon. Ian A. Mackenzie. This copy, dated December 15 of last year, contains the following:
Throughout its proceedings the committee has adopted a purely non-partisan approach to all questions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: In effect, I said the same thing last night.

This was an article explaining the purpose of the committee on veterans affairs. It gave the same impression as the one I had received up to last Christmas. On numerous occasions I quoted that same paragraph. I quoted it, and with pride, when I was speaking to the various branches of the Canadian Legion in my own constituency at Christmas time, because I believed it reflected the true attitude of the committee on veterans affairs up to that time. But there has come a change in the attitude adopted in the com-

mittee-or perhaps I should say by certain members of the committee-during this session. I think one might divide the committee into two parts. There are what I would call the regular attendants, those who are able to put to one side their other parliamentary business in order to devote their main attention to the matters affecting the veterans whose affairs are being discussed by the committee. I say that those regular attendants are still adopting a strictly non-partisan attitude. Liberal members have spoken against other Liberal members. C.C.P., Social Creditors and members of the Progressive Conservative party have not been afraid to express views different from those held by other members of their own particular political persuasions. I believe each man has spoken in the light of his experience. I believe each has voted, when votes have been called, in accordance with his own good, sound judgment.
Those regular attendants have listened to briefs presented by various veteran organizations throughout Canada. They have heard hours and hours of evidence given by officials of the different departments. They have listened to speeches by their chairman which have been both tense and sincere. If at times they have been rather long and perhaps a little difficult to follow because of repetition, we have always credited our chairman with great sincerity and earnestness of purpose.
After serious discussion, various recommendations have been made, not always unanimously but always with the vote of the majority of those attending that committee. Then, on some occasions the committee has gone into camera sittings, when the attitude of the government has been explained.

In order to make clear my attitude respecting the principle involved in the resolution, I should like to point out that after these camera sittings of the committee to which I have just referred, and the proceedings of which I pass over without comment, the government came down and explained its attitude. The committee then reassembled and conferred with the idea of seeing whether it was possible to come to an agreement, because the Minister of Veterans Affairs repeatedly asked the committee if at all possible to reach a unanimous opinion. There was a desire in the committee to cooperate. Unfortunately some of the later conferences reminded me of conferences I held when I was in the army, which were more on the type of an order group than what is generally meant by a conference in which discussions are held. At those meetings I would adopt the attitude and say, "Gentlemen, I have told you my plan, are there any questions? If not, thank you very much, that is all." In other words, take it or leave it. If, however, the committee was not prepared to accept all the recommendations of the government, then there would be
whining and bellowing much the same as there was last night. Questions which had been settled would be reopened. The Liberal whip would appear at the door, heads would be counted, and back-benchers and cabinet ministers would slide into their places. New recommendations were made. I shall come definitely to the principle of the resolution. We were asked repeatedly last night whether we were in favour of the resolution. I am not in favour of the resolution. We were asked last night whether we would accept the responsibility of asking to have the resolution withdrawn. I accept the responsibility of asking to have the resolution withdrawn, provided that the government will give an honourable understanding that before the close of this session it will bring down a new bill giving more generous terms to these old soldiers whom we are now considering. I am not in favour of any bill that is only a half measure.
I ask the parliamentary assistant to notice the words I used, " giving more generous terms." I do not know how far he and the government are prepared to go in that respect. It has been suggested that these old soldiers be given clear title after twenty or twenty-five years to the land they obtained through the soldier settlement board. All the arguments in favour of granting such free title have been presented, such as the age that these men have reached, their inability to find a place in the labour market and the fact that many of them left their farms to serve in home defence units, such as the veterans guard and security guard and so forth, and rendered valuable service during world war II, but suffered additional infirmities because of the exposure they underwent. All these have been advanced.
It has been pointed out also that partly because their service was in Canada only, partly because they have already received some consideration from the soldier settlement board, and partly because of their age, they are not entitled to receive all the benefits of the Veterans Land Act. The attitude of the government in this connection is having an effect upon young veterans of this war who are considering going on the land. That statement is borne out by the figures which were tabled last March showing that up to March 31 only
5,000	out of hundreds of thousands of returned men had actually taken out the full farm benefits under the Veterans Land Act. This is attributable to many causes, one of which is the feeling that their fathers did not get a square deal from the soldier settlement board.
I take it the government is anxious to establish on the land as many veterans as possible. Let us give them encouragement. It has been suggested that these young men will prefer to wait for twenty-five years knowing that they will receive something for

nothing, and because they have the example of some poor old soldier of the first great war who lived in hardship for that length of time and who had some of his indebtedness remitted by a generous government I do not believe that those who advance that type of argument are in touch with young Canada at all. I think they have failed entirely to interpret the determination of the veteran of this war to get reestablished and to continue to do something for the service of his country.
The government may not feel inclined to give clear title. The government may feel that it cannot write off all the soldier settler's indebtedness. We are having examples of t'he government writing off very considerable sums, examples of government moneys being spent to buy equipment which afterwards was sold for a song. Be that as it may there are other ways in which more generous treatment could be accorded to these old soldiers. Their indebtedness might be reduced. There is plenty of time yet to reconsider during this session the bill which is to be placed before the house. Other bills far more complicated than this one have been withdrawn at the eleventh hour of the session, rewritten, brought down again and passed. Therefore I ask the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs whether he is prepared now to withdraw the resolution, on the understanding that it will be brought down again this session in such form as to give more generous terms to these old soldier settlers. If he is not prepared to give that undertaking, then it may be that I shall be forced' to vote for the resolution, because I do not want to stand in the way of any soldier getting even the small additional advantage that this meagre resolution offers to him.

Mr. Speaker, I fancy that I am in a unique position in rising to speak on this resolution, not because of my attitude toward the resolution itself, but because of the fact that so far the discussion has had little or nothing to do with the subject matter of the resolution.
I am one of those who in this house a year ago advocated the granting of clear title, for reasons which I gave at the time. I think it is uneconomic to send good money after bad. If we are not going to leave it to the house and the people of this country to read the proceedings of the committee, I am entitled to say on my own behalf that when a member of the committee brought forward a resolution to grant clear title I supported it. I think that was the only recorded vote that has taken place in the veterans committee in the last two parliaments. My word on that can-

Soldier Settlement
not be questioned. While I lost my vote on that resolution, I was one of those who, in spite of all the whining and bellowing which the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) mentioned, and now the braying which has followed it, accepted unanimously this much, that we have in the resolution now before us.
I have been a member of the veterans' committee since it was first established after the elections of 1935, except for a few breaks during 1941 and 1942. I have boasted across this country to the legionnaires of Canada and their families and friends that the veterans' committee was one committee in which members drawn from every corner of the house had sat together and done their best to interpret the generosity and good w'ill of the people of Canada to the veterans of Canada without any resort to politics. I will say that with certain lamentable exceptions we have been singularly free from party politics in the veterans' committee, and I am proud of that.
I have to agree with the hon. member for Nanaimo when he says that party lines have frequently been cut across in the veterans committee with respect to soldier legislation. Why in heaven's name, when we have before us now a resolution embodying a concession to the soldier settlers which I admit is less than on two occasions I advocated in the veterans committee, there should be an attempt, as there has been in the last fifteen minutes, to play politics, a bald-faced attempt to play the cheapest electioneering kind of politics, is something I cannot understand. I have no hesitation in saying that. I invite anybody to read the record. This is my thirteenth session; I have been completely free from personalities in this house, and I want to keep my record that way. I have given most of my time outside of the chamber to the veterans committee, and I have been proud of the associations I have had with the friends of the soldiers who have been members of that committee.
This resolution, unsatisfactory as it was to some of us, was adopted unanimously. Why should a resolution adopted unanimously by the committee be used as an opportunity to bring on a political Donnybrook in this house at the expense of the people to whom we owe so much? That is not good enough, and I protest against it with all the sincerity of which I am capable. I understand the game of politics, and I am perfectly free to meet my hon. friends opposite on any committee dealing with any subject other than soldiers affairs, but in the veterans committee politics has been excluded and we have made a contribution that has been worth while to the
welfare of the soldiers. I resent most keenly, as most members of the committee will resent and the veterans themselves who understand what is being done for them in this resolution will resent, the tone and tenor of this whole debate.

Mr. Speaker, not being a veteran I think you should hear a word from me on this subject. I am amazed at the attempt of members on the other side of the house to shift the responsibility on to the shoulders of others when they themselves were responsible for giving these settlers the worst soldier rehabilitation legislation this country ever had. They placed these soldier settlers on land that was growing nothing but jack-pine. The soldier settlers had to cut the jack-pine for a living, and when the jack-pine ran out they had to snare rabbits. Placing the veterans on such poor land, with such poor machinery, and under such poor conditions we could not expect them to be in any other position than the one they are in now. I feel that the government is doing everything possible for these veterans in the circumstances in which others have placed them; therefore I resent the attempt at this time to infringe on the right of the government to accept the responsibiliy which has been placed upon them by the people of this country.
It just shows you the difference. It shows you the advantages which the boys of this war have, and proves that the government of to-day has the war veterans at heart in every respect. Care has been taken in the purchase of the farms with which these men have been provided, to see that they are productive. Throughout the neighbourhood in which I live they have been bought at prices not exceeding S30 an acre; in the last war, on the other hand, prices were paid all the way up to $50 and $60 an acre. Now the boys have not had to pay as much, and their circumstances are altogether different. It has also been provided that out-of-work benefits shall be given the men so that they may not have to spend their gratuities, and those who were obliged to suspend their education are now enabled to resume it.
' Once more, to cut the matter short, I would say that this matter has been dealt with in the committee; therefore it would be advisable for us to refrain from threshing old straw so that we shall not be here until Christmas.

Since this matter has been brought up, I should like to make plain the position of a number of members in this group in regard to the resolution. As one who is a veteran of the first
Soldier Settlement

world war, I took a great interest in the soldier settlement scheme. I have lived among, and on occasions I have lived with, members of the fighting forces who took up land under the old soldier settlement board scheme, and resolution after resolution has appeared on the order paper of this house asking the government to grant free title to the soldiers of the last war who are still on the land. Now, in order that the house may get a proper picture of the success or failure of that scheme, I would ask the parliamentary assistant, who is now piloting this resolution through the house, to put on the record the number of men, originally 25,000, who under the old soldier settlement board scheme have lost their farms through foreclosure, or deserted them entirely, or were compelled to sign quit claim deeds. The fact that a very small percentage, about twenty per cent, now remain on the land, many of them still in debt, is an indictment from which no government can escape by argument. It is the failure to make that old soldier board settlement scheme work that we protest against.
I know that since this war started these men, who are now approaching the last years of their lives, when they can do little actual hard labour on the farm, have done a remarkable job, and the little group who are left are paying off what they can with the returns they receive, which have been somewhat increased as a result of the war situation.
Let me give some actual cases from my own constituency. First I will take the case of a man near the town- of Raymore. These are his cash returns over a period of years. According to the contract he had, he was supposed to pay to the board every year the sum of $225. In 1935 his gross receipts were $350. His harvesting and threshing expenses and taxes amounted to $150, leaving him, for the maintenance of his home and to carry on, the sum of $200. In 1936 his gross receipts were $396, and his expenses were $150, which left him $240 for maintenance of the home. In 1937 his total receipts for the whole farm amounted to just $33, while taxes and repairs -there was no threshing bill because the crop was so small-left him with a loss of $50 on the year's operations. In 1938 he had an income of $274 and expenses of $150, so that he had $124 for the year to keep his family. In 1939 his gross receipts were $620, and he was repaying relief obtained during the years when he tried to carry on with practically no farm income. After paying for repairs to barn and so on he had net proceeds of $354. Imagine that man trying to carry on over the years on less than $1,000 a year! And the next year we find the soldier settlement board

clamping down on him, sending inspectors to investigate. I took the matter up because this man was in despair. They were advertising his land for sale because he had not paid the $225 every year.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Did he apply under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act or under P.C. 10472?
What good does that do? He is losing his land.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Others who did apply were given a very good adjustment. I wondered whether the hon. member had advised this gentleman to take advantage of the assistance provided either by legislation or by order in council.
If I had thought he could maintain control of his land and have an equity in it with any future hope of getting title to it, I would so advise him.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Did you?
Yes, I did.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: And did he get a satisfactory settlement?

He got a partial settlement, but not before his land was offered for sale. I have another case before me. Apparently the records got twisted in the central office in Saskatoon, and they sent a letter to this man on January 16, 1941, pointing out to him that the amount of his arrears in taxes was $458. But he had cash receipts for taxes or had worked them out in labour; nevertheless they concluded their letter as follows:
We are definitely notifying you now that if this quit claim deed is not completed and returned to this office prior to the 13th of February that you will leave us no option but to recommend to our head office the immediate rescission of your contract. We are, therefore, hoping that you will return quit claim deed as soon as possible.
Another man encountered difficulties, after doing the best he could. He received particularly embarrassing instructions when he had the sum of $130 left from the year's operations and found it necessary to take his wife to hospital because she was suffering from cancer. She had to receive treatment every month, and this used up practically all the resources he had; then he received from the soldier settlement board notification to the effect that he must try to make further payments. Going back to the year 1925, this man has had gross receipts of $1,491 and payments to the soldier settlement board of $237 each year. His average income has been $783, while he has made payments in other respects each year amounting to $170 from

Soldier Settlement
the very small crops that he has had. Having a family to support, he found it almost impossible to carry on the year's operations, and yet the soldier settlement board hounded him from day to day, taking advantage, as it appeared to him, of the situation in which he found himself, to press him when he was least able to pay, thus humiliating him and putting him in a position where he nearly lost- his land.
Near the town of Togo one man took up land with two other veterans of the last war. The boys on either side of him gave up in despair because they could not make a go of it, but this man carried on. His wife stayed on the farm, and he filed on another homestead in the north. He operated his little farm as best he could. He went out and proved the other land in the northern part of the country. He finally sold that and took all the money he had and put it in the quarter-section which he had near Togo. He still found himself terrifically in arrears. The administrative office must know that the men who are left on the land cannot now carry on the necessary work and make their proposition pay. To give a reduction of interest rates under the new contract for twenty years is not giving very much to men who are sixty-five years old. Surely for the remainder of the veterans it is not asking for a hand-out; it is asking only for justice that these men be granted a free title to their land. After all, these men have suffered much. I have talked to men who were turned off their land in the bad years by the soldier settlement board. The bitterness in their hearts about the treatment they received from governments over the years when income was small is something which will live long in their memory and in that of their children and their children's children. They will never forget the treatment which has been handed out by this board.
If this scheme is as successful as the parliamentary assistant seems to imply, where are the 15.000 men who started out on it? They gave to it the best years of their work, and they have nothing. Of the 25,000 who started out. 5.000 are left, but I am talking of the
15,000	to whom this scheme was nothing but complete failure. What they think of the treatment accorded to them by the governments of this country is something which one would hate to express. These men gave the best of their lives in the last war; they worked through years when there was no possibility of anyone making a sufficient income even to maintain himself, to say nothing of being held responsible for large payments on the land. I know that reductions were made; I know that certain adjustments were also made.
Although the burden was lifted, there was still too much left upon them to make it possible for them to carry on, and the failure of the vast majority is the thing to which we must give our attention.
I am suggesting that you cannot always take the decisions of one particular province. The parliamentary assistant made some reference to the representatives of the British Empire Service League and what conclusions they had arrived at in one particular province. I have found on examining these things that very often in the smaller centres the soldier settler could not make his voice heard. He did not have the opportunity to go to 'his veterans' meeting or to carry his story to the central organization. In the larger centres it often happened that government officials took charge of the work and gained control of many of the official positions in the British Empire Service League; therefore government policy was always protected. But the boys in the remote areas had no means of making their voices heard, and in a good many cases the problems of the soldier settlers have not been heard. Many of these boys are now scattered and employed in various parts of Canada, and they have no voice in the decisions of the British Empire Service League. The British Empire Service League may pass resolutions at provincial convention which do not take into account the representations of these men who suffered and are now passing out of the picture. I had one case drawn to my attention of a soldier who had bought one of the soldier settler farms. He was receiving a pension on account of an amputation or disability incurred during the war. This pension could not be touched in any way so far as payments were concerned, but he was asked to assign a part of his pension to take care of the rent for his farm, since he had not been able to make the ordinary payments. That is the kind of treatment which makes the opposition in the house demand that the government recognize the failure of the scheme and grant these burnt-out men clear titles to their land, so that in the few remaining years of their lives they may live in peace and without worry.

I rise to a point of order. On several occasions last evening the hon. member for Rosthem (Mr. Tucker) said that the committee was unanimous in reporting this resolution. The hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) made the same statement to-day. I should like to call the attention of the house to the fact that this resolution has been on the order paper since April 12, which is over two and a half months ago. I
Soldier Settlement

understand that the reason it was not brought before the house sooner was that the committee had hoped to include other recommendations in this resolution. As the parliamentary assistant knows, two or three other proposals were made in the committee, and the committee had hoped they would be included in the resolution. After two and a half months we find that the resolution now appears before the house in the form in which it was presented on April 12, in spite of the fact that considerable discussion has since taken place in the committee, and in spite of the fact that hon. members made certain motions to have other principles included in the resolution. That, I am sure, is a clear indication to the house that the committee was not unanimous as far as this resolution is concerned. We wanted more included. I make this statement to keep the record straight. We are in favour of the two matters which are raised in the resolution, but we did want and we insisted in the committee that other matters be included. I do not think it is fair to hon. members of the committee who fought to have other principles included to say now that we were unanimous on this resolution.

On the point of order, since the hon. member has quoted me with respect to this resolution, I was careful to say that this resolution did not embody all that some members of the committee, including myself, wanted. But having failed to achieve that, I said, and I repeat, that having decided in the committee that we were not going to get all that we asked for, the committee unanimously agreed to request that which this resolution asks for.
The hon. member cannot put that on the record-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. There is no point of order before the house.

I wish to place before the house my views on this matter, because I happen to be the sole Progressive Conservative member for Saskatchewan. The hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) has given the government's point of view, and other members have expressed the views of the C.C.F. party. The stand taken by the Progressive Conservative party in Saskatchewan is that there should be a discharge of the indebtedness of all soldier settlers holding contracts since the first great war.
Some hon. members say that the Canadian Legion in Saskatchewan is not in favour of that. I realize that the provincial association

did not support it, but individual branches all over the province have supported it. The branch in Prince Albert, to which I belong, supported it, and the president of the provincial command is Mr. Walter Whalen, one time president of the Prince Albert branch, and latterly the representative there.
I can see no argument against granting this right to men who have suffered as few others have suffered under similar circumstances during the last twenty-five years. I have visited with them, as have other hon. members. They have gone through difficulties the like of which those who are not acquainted with the circumstances under which they live do not appreciate. There can be no argument against it on the ground of repudiation of debt, because we have the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act which regularly reduces and often entirely discharges debt.
So far as any saving to the country is concerned, last evening the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) stated that the director had said in evidence that the cost of administering the soldier settlement indebtedness amounted to some 8100,000 a year. Certainly it must have decreased recently, because in a return brought down in 1944 the cost of administration of the soldier settlement indebtedness in the preceding year was given as $646,000. If the remaining indebtedness is amortized over a period of twenty-five years under the order in council pertinent to this matter is will cost to collect the balance of the indebtedness three times as much as is actually owing to-day, on the basis of the figures given in 1943.
There is one other matter I want to mention. I may be in disagreement with other hon. members on this side of the house, but I do not believe the Veterans Land Act is being administered as it should be in the province of Saskatchewan.
Or any other province.

Or any other province. I hear more criticism of this department than of any other department. It seems to be paralysed by red tape. I know in my own province those who administer it are discriminating as against certain productive sections. It is impossible to get any action-and any criticism I have to offer I express when the person concerned is present. I have often said to the minister, "You accept the recommendations we make. You give them every consideration. You turn them over to the administrator of the Veterans Land Act, and there they die." Let me give an example. In my constituency, areas that have been pro-

Soldier Settlement
ductive ever since the C.P.R. came to western Canada are denied the privilege of having soldier settlers.

the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefen-baker) was speaking to a point of order, but I think I have heard enough on this point. Last evening I drew the attention of hon. members to the fact that the house was considering a certain resolution to amend the Soldier Settlement Act, and requested hon. members to make their remarks relevant to that act. All I can do is repeat that request this afternoon.

With the greatest deference, Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling. I was trying to show that if the same people are administering the present act who administered the Soldier Settlement Act, one can well understand the difficulties some of these soldier settlers have experienced in recent years; and I was just trying to discuss the principle before the house at the moment.
So far as the resolution is concerned, I advocated this in the house in 1941. It is not something new. I believe the first person to interest himself in behalf of the old settlers, in securing a reduction in the interest rate from 5 per cent to 3^ per cent in order to place them on the same basis as those coming under the Veterans Land Act, was Mr. Campbell of the Edmonton Bulletin, who urged this action over a very considerable period of time. We are in favour of this resolution as it stands, but surely we are permitted to say that it does not go far enough.
There is just one other point in that connection. In your experience, sir, have you ever heard a responsible administrator on the government side of the house say that when the opposition says, "We support this as far as it goes but it does not go far enough," they then should be told that the government might take away the resolution because we ask for more than it covers? That is a denial of the independence of parliament and of the rights of members of parliament.
Oh, oh.

Oh, yes; my hon. friends have used threats like that before; that is why they are so jocular about it, but we are not one bit frightened by threats like that. So far as we are concerned we believe this is a proper resolution. We feel that it does not go far enough, and we are not going to be intimidated by any suggestion that if we ask that it go farther, the resolution will be withdrawn.

Mr. Speaker, I have not taken part in the discussion of these matters for some years, be-
Soldier Settlement

cause we now have in the house a large number of returned men who have been overseas and who know something about the condition of those who went on the land after the first war, as well as those who have gone on the land since the end of the last war. I have received a large number of letters, however, from soldiers who were told wonderful things about what the dominion and provincial governments were going to do for those who went on the land. I thought the committee would have brought in a report which would be much more liberal toward those concerned, because as you know, Mr. Speaker, between the two wars there was continuous complaint about the difficulties and hardships of those who had gone on the land.
This idea of granting land was first carried out, I think, after the northwest rebellion, and was continued after the Fenian raid, *when grants of land were given by the dominion and the provinces. Some of those people, however, never saw the land and got shabby treatment, though in Ontario I understand they were given 160 acres. As everyone knows, the soldier who goes on the land has a hard job. Many of them had not been farmers; many had to put up with conditions which no individual should have to endure. I used to visit this committee once in a while, and in other years it was one committee which left out politics and thought first, last and always of how the returned men could be helped. These people suffered greatly through the lack of transportation and the lack of proper appliances and conveniences with which to work, though this condition has been helped through the rural electrification movement in one or two of the provinces. I was in hopes that the committee would cut out all this red tape and the technicalities which we have seen since the debate started, and that the matter might be referred back to the committee so that it could make a more liberal appropriation.
True, some help has been given by way of a reduced rate of interest. I have had letters from some who wanted to go on the land but who, after they had written and taken the matter up. declined to go any further.
I hope we shall have better success in putting men back on the land1 after the second war than we did after the first one, because conditions have been growing worse, in geometrical progression, ever since the first war. Complaints	have been made by one
and all who	went	on	the	land.	We hear talkabout going	back	to	the	land;	well, who isgoing to go	back	to	the	land,	after serving
in the second world war, if he has to put

up with the intolerable conditions suffered by those who went back to the land after the first war?
While undoubtedly the chairman of the committee is most active, I suggest he is too technical; and if he wishes to have this resolution passed he is going the wrong way about it. I can tell you this, that I receive as many letters from soldiers as any other member and many of them refer to this particular matter. These men have come back from the second world war. I do hope the committee will consider much more liberal treatment of those who wish to go back on the land after fighting a second world war.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take any considerable time in what I have to say, because I shall subscribe to what other hon. members have said. I am a member of the legion, and also have been on a soldier settlement farm, so I know something about it.
I do wish to go on record, however, in support of what the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair), the hon. member for Mel-fort (Mr. Wright) and other hon. members have said. I have letters from members of the legion in Manitoba complaining repeatedly about the Veterans Land Act. There seems to be something wrong there. Men who wish to come under the settlement scheme have difficulty in buying farms in communities where they have lived all their days. Surely there must be something wrong with that. If anyone knows conditions in a community, surely it must be the man who was born and raised there.
When a man reaches the age of twenty-four or twenty-five he finds that he wants to buy a farm, but the administrators of the Veterans Land Act say, "No, you cannot settle here." Surely the young man himself should be the best judge of that. I do not wish to take further time, but desire only to support what other hon. members from Manitoba have said.

Mr. Speaker, despite the numerous occasions upon which attention has been drawn to the terms of the resolution, the fact remains that the debate has hinged on the question of free titles being given to veterans of the war of 1914-18, who settled under soldier settlement legislation of that time. The debate has revolved almost completely around the refusal of the government to accede to that request. The government, apparently having decided definitely against that course, I would ask them at least to give to these old soldiers some better treatment, some better reward than that

Soldier Settlement
provided in the resolution before the house. Requests from a considerable number of these veterans that they be given free title to their lands have originated, I believe, from the fact that many parcels of land after being taken back from settlers by the soldier settlement board were then resold to civilians on much better terms than -were given the soldier settler. I believe that has been the cause of much of the trouble.
In my view most soldier settlers would be reasonably well satisfied if the Soldier Settlement Act were amended in such fashion as to give them as good treatment respecting their debts on their farms as ordinary civilians have received after those farms have been taken away from the soldier settlers.
I have here from a soldier settler in Alberta a letter which, I believe, illustrates extremely well what has been going on and the reasons for discontent which now exist. This letter is dated March 7, 1946, and states:
During the month of April, 1943, the soldier settlement board sold the above parcel of land to Mr. X of Lougheed, Alta., for $160 cash and Mr. X assumed the outstanding taxes which amounted to $70. In other words he receives a clear title to this quarter section for $230 or 17 per cent of its assessed value. Below is a general description of this quarter, and also a few facts concerning this ease.
1.	It contains 160 acres assessed at $1,340.
By the municipal assessors.
2.	Of this amount there is from 110 to 115 acres of fairly level medium black sand loam with a clay subsoil. There is also another 15 to 20 acres of very heavy rolling land of the same type in the north and east portion, making a total of at least 125 acres of arable land.
3.	The balance is classed as pasture land of varying contour; but for the most part low-lying land of mixed soil furnishing a good natural pasture.
4.	There is also a spring on this quarter, an unfailing source of fresh water.
5.	At present there is .about 45 acres cultivated, but the balance of the arable land can be easily broken as it is practically free of rock and contains only about 15 acres of light willow and poplar brush which can also be easily broken up.
6.	This quarter is situated in the municipal district of Asquith, about 125 miles southeast of Edmonton. It is five and one-half miles from a village with six grain elevators and a full grade 12 high school, three and one-half miles off of provincial gravelled highway No. 13, two and one-half miles from a rural school.
7.	It is fully fenced and is bounded on the south and east by rural telephone line.
This farm was originally under contract by a veteran of the first great war, who together with one of his sons, served overseas on active service, in this second war. I've inquired of the board if he or any of his family was given the chance to repurchase this farm at this price. From their reply they have a quit claim from him and so far as he was concerned the incident was closed. No other vet of either the first or
present war was given an opportunity to purchase this farm at this price. I have also asked the board if the same reduction in value would be given the soldier settlers.
That, I think, would solve this whole question in a fairly satisfactory way, namely, if in cases of this kind the same reduction in land value were given as is given when the land is subsequently sold to an ordinary civilian. Then, to continue with the letter:
From their reply this can't be done. They can't lower the valuation to a settler, but once they receive a quit claim they have the power to revalue and can sell it to some other party for any price they mutually agree upon.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member knows, of course, that under P.C. 10472 that is incorrect.

That is not the case. I took up this matter with the director of the soldier settlement board, Mr. Murchison and was informed by him that this statement is correct when it states that the soldier settlement board is not able to lower the valuation to a settler, although once they have obtained a quit claim from the settler they can sell the land for any figure they please.
In this particular case I made a further request that Mr. Murchison look into the matter, and the application of P.C. 10472, to which the parliamentary assistant has just referred, in order to have a revaluation and a reduction in this man's indebtedness. I have not the figure here, but I believe it stands at about $2,000. This was done, and the reply from the board was that it was impossible to make any reduction other than that which had already been made. At the same time this man offered the board $500 as a settlement of the amount owing them. That was more than twice the amount that the neighbouring quarter-section had been sold for, after it was taken away from another veteran.
Will the hon. member tell me when the quit claim was given in the first place, and the name of the writer of the letter?

I shall be glad to give all the names, if you wish. The writer of the letter is Mr. E. M. Petersen. The first paragraph of the letter stated that the land was sold in April, 1943. If the hon. member had been listening a little more closely he would not have needed to ask the question. To continue with the letter:
This is certainly a ridiculous state of affairs and leaves everything open to graft and favouritism. Now, who is the purchaser to receive a plum of this kind? The party in question came to this country about 25 years ago. He is considered to be a good farmer, a good neighbour and has a good eye for bargains. If he is naturalized it wouldn't be until 1935, at which
Soldier Settlement

time many were debating whether to qualify for the $25 per month or retain the status of citizenship of the country of their origin.
He goes on to tell more about this man which I do not think is of any particular interest; then he says:
The S.S.B. sells him this farm at a time of guaranteed prices for farm products. Any of the following items gave him a clear title to this land: two two-year old steers, nine hogs, 250 bushels of wheat, 400 bushels of barley or 500 bushels of oats which gives him an ideal mixed farming half section. It will be hard to convince him that there isn't a Santa Claus from now on as long as there is a S.S.B. in Edmonton and especially since he has resold this quarter for $1,350 cash. This deal was also negotiated at a time when the government was proposing various plans for rehabilitation of vets of this last war. From any report I have been able to get they are asking the present vets more for one or two acres of land adjoining some city or fifteen times as much for a quarter section as what the S.S.B. asked and received from this party, while they were away fighting for this country of which it is doubtful if he has become a citizen.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Has the hon. member
looked into th*e facts alleged in this letter, and does he say on his own responsibility as a member they are correct, or is he just reading something that has been written to him?
I can give you one exactly the same.

I have looked into the facts, and I have had a solicitor in Calgary look into the facts, and I am prepared to state on my responsibility as a member that they are correct. I took this matter up with Mr. Murchison some six weeks ago, and he did not dispute the facts which I have given. I am not blaming Mr. Murchison in the slightest, and I want that understood. Mr. Murchison's position is that he must administer the act under the provisions as laid down. The provisions of the act do not permit the soldier settlement board to write off a man's indebtedness to the figure which his land would bring in the open market. They just cannot do that, and that is what is required. This man goes on to say:
Personally, I'm taking the stand that if the government can afford to take a loss of several thousand dollars to supply Mr. X with a quarter section. I feel that we, the old settlers, should be dealt with on the same terms and do not intend making any further payments until I get a satisfactory answer on how these values were arrived at not only in this case but also in regards to the sale by the S.S.B. of S.W. quarter of Section 11-43-11 west of the 4th which took place about the same time only in this case, the party purchasing same while he also was military exempt in both wars, buys this land, 187 acres with buildings and a well, for $200 or for about one-sixth of the assessed value which in this case was $1,158, as in the previous instance the board took a loss of several thousand dollars.
[Mr. Harkness.l
Mr. Petersen, who writes this letter, is not asking to have his debt forgiven. He says that most of the soldier settlers in his area and other men whom he knows are not asking to have their debts completely forgiven. What they want is a reasonable deal. What they want is a deal as good as that given to the ordinary civilian, as good as that given, according to information, the corrections of which I do not know, to men who actually fought against them in the last war, members of the German army. Those men came to Canada and are able to buy land from the soldier settlement board at a much lower figure than a soldier settler can buy it for himself. That is what these men want. In most cases they are not asking for the total obliteration of debt; they just want a square deal, which they have not had.
I call upon the government, as the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) has done, to write into the Soldier Settlement Act provisions which will enable a soldier settler to obtain land held by him for an amount equal to what the land would sell for if taken away and sold to an ordinary civilian.

I rise simply to apologize to the hon. member for interrupting. I thought the crux of this particular case was the length of time the land was in
the hands of the board, and I asked for the date of the quit claim.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I could not answer the questions asked by the hon. member for Yorkton until we were in committee. I have a statement, it is not as complete as I would like. However, I think it will be of interest to the committee.
There were originally 24,793 soldier settlers with contracts. Of that number, 6,635 contracts were terminated either by voluntary abandonment, by notice of rescission by death, or because of domestic difficulties, up to January 1, 1926. From that date until January 1, 1932, there were another 6,244 terminations. Of the original 24,793, there were therefore 12,879 whose contracts were terminated by January 1, 1932. From that date to the present, that is during the past fourteen years, there have been 946 terminations of contracts. Of the 946 terminations, five took place during 1945 and 1946. My hon. friend is interested to know how many of them were voluntary, how many were actually based on rescission, and so on. I am told by the board that it is utterly impossible to provide that information, that during the difficult thirties, parti-

Soldier Settlement
cularly the early thirties, there were so many settlers who could not possibly make a living on some of these farms that they left them and they could not be found to ascertain whether they were willing to give a quit-claim or not, and so to clear up the situation formal notice of rescission had to be given. I understand that many of these were actual cases of abandonment and that a good proportion were quit-claims.
Does that include the number who gave a quit-claim and then returned and rented the farm?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: It includes the entire number who signed quit-claims. If they entered into a new agreement I could not- say for certain whether they are included in the number of those who actually threw up their land. The figures that were most interesting to me were those which showed that during the last fourteen years actually less than one thousand gave up their lands. Were those rescissions? *

speechtext:
If I might say a word or two, it is all very well for a general statement to be made, but when you come to a particular district you find out what is actually being done and how the thing is working out. In the particular district that I have mentioned there are three farms, close to one another. Their assessed value by the municipal assessor was comparable. The assessment of the man I mentioned this afternoon
