Soldier Settlement

was higher, but not very much higher, than that of the other two, chiefly because at his own expense he had put up considerably better buildings. As the thing actually worked out, this land was sold in 1943, when land values should have been higher than in 194041, at the figure which I mentioned, as nearly as I could determine, and which was not disputed by Mr. Murchison. I think that is evidence in itself that the soldier settler has not been given the deal which you and I and probably many others thought he was being given under the order in council. The land is only worth what it can be sold for in the district on the open market, and apparently all that could be got for these two quarter-sections, according to the director's statement, was $200 and $230 respectively. At the same time the other man's assessment was reduced $600. As I understand it, he owed less than either of the other two men, who had been induced to sign quit-claims and had left the land.

I want to thank the parliamentary assistant for giving me those figures. In 1942 there was placed on the records of this house, in reply to a question of mine, the following facts with regard to Saskatchewan. I believe there were 6,164 settlers settled in Saskatchewan under the Soldier Settlement Act and at that time they incurred an indebtedness of $25,576,000 in rough thousands. In 1942 there were 2,308 still on the land. I asked for the original indebtedness of the 2,308 still on the land and was advised that the information could not be obtained but that they could give it for the accounts from one office, namely, 730. The figures regarding these are interesting. For the 730 accounts they gave me, the original indebtedness was roughly $2,839,000. Then I asked how much in the form of payments these men had given up to date. For these 730 accounts referred to, the information was that they had made payments of $1,508,000. I asked what was the present indebtedness of these men, and I found that in spite of the fact that they owed only $2,830,000 and they had paid $1,508,000, their indebtedness as at January 1, 1942, was $3,864,000. They were indebted originally in the sum of $2,800,000, had paid $1,500,000 or a little oyer half, and now they were $1,000,000 more in debt than when they started.
I put these figures on the record so that people can see the type of burden under which these men have been carrying on and the reason why they lost hope, and therefore why special consideration should be given to such people, in view of all the hardships

they have gone through. It must have been because of the burden imposed upon them that they found it impossible to carry on. Had they been given an opportunity of paying the debt which they had incurred, and which they wanted to repay during those years from 1936 to 1940, it is quite evident that, if they could pay $1,500,000 up to 1942, they would have paid off the whole thing. What they are now asked to pay represents a burden of $1,000,000 more than that with which they started; that is, speaking of the 730. That is an example of what I mean when I say that this sort of thing requires special consideration at this time. Had they been paying off in ordinary times, their indebtedness would have been more than paid.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: What page is the hon. gentleman referring to?

I will send a copy to the minister. It was tabled in 1942. That is the basis on which we make our request. It is not a matter of political pressure, as the hon. member tried to imply last night. It is a matter of seeing that justice is done. These men do not ask for a hand-out; they are asking for a square deal. Certainly, after what they have done, they are entitled to such a deal and their case should be taken into consideration.

Last evening my time had expired before I was able to conclude my presentation of the subject and I should like now to continue it. I wish to refer to page 1007 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the special committee on veterans affairs of Tuesday, June 18, when the following resolution was proposed by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. McKay):
That all soldier settlers who took up land under the soldier settlement hoard be granted clear title to such lands as of March 31, 1944; that clear title be also granted to the widows, children, or dependents of such soldier settlers; and that in the case of veteran settlers who have been dispossessed of their lands during the period between September 3, 1939 and March 31, 1944, either by quit claim or by eviction, such lands be restored and clear title granted to the settler, or adequate compensation made to him.
Immediately after this the Minister of Veterans Affairs had this to say, as reported at page 1009:
Mr. Chairman, I should like an opportunity to say a word. Speaking on behalf of the government, we are definitely opposed to this clear title suggestion for several reasons, and I will state them very briefly and very succinctly. In the first place, the concession of $2,320 given the settlers under the present act is not equal to the various repeated concessions that were given to the old soldier settlers after 1919.

Soldier Settlement
My reply to that argument is that the concessions given to the settlers under the soldier settlement board can never compensate for the disadvantages under which they were placed. By that I mean that when the settlers bought the land, live stock and equipment, wheat was worth from $2.50 to $3 a bushel, milch cows from $125 to $150 apiece, and work horses, which most of the settlers used at that time, were worth from $350 to $400 a team. Shortly after that, however, the price of wheat had dropped away below the dollar mark; the price of milch cows was $25 each, and you could get all the horses you wanted at $25 each. At the same time the interest of five per cent on current accounts and seven per cent on arrears went on and was carried on the books against these farmer's. So that the concessions which were granted would not compensate for the differences in valuation, over which the government had complete control if they wanted to exercise it. Going on, the minister said:
I admit with my friend that prices were too high. I admit that the interest rates were too high. But concessions were made, and I think that the suggestion contained in the amendment is absolutely unfair and inequitable. It is not fair to the boys who have paid up and who are paying up to-day in advance. They are paying up hundreds of thousands of dollars in advance, the old soldier settlers, the men who have really worked and are working upon their farms.
That statement, I suggest, is too small for a big man like the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I find in it the insinuation that the fellows who have not yet paid their debts are not working as hard as they should. Well, as one who has lived under similar conditions and who has pleaded before for these men, I can say that they work from twelve to sixteen hours a day, work harder than any of us around here have ever worked in our lives and under worse conditions, and they were much more poorly fed than a number of us who are here. Continuing, the minister said:
If you give clear title to the men who have not worked so hard, you are working an injustice upon the fellows who worked hard upon their farms.
In answer to that, I would say that you are imposing just a little less injustice upon the fellows who would receive clear title than those who have already paid. By giving clear titles as of March 31, 1944, you will be easing up a little on the hardship that has been inflicted upon them during the past twenty-seven years. To continue with the minister's statement:
Secondly, you are wrecking the whole system of administration under the present Veterans Land Act if you are going to give clear title to the old soldier settlers.
Mr. McKay:	Oh, no.
Hon. Mr. Mackenzie:	Oh, yes, you are.
Mr. McKay:	In what respect?
Hon. Mr. Mackenzie: You are held up in this case because they may not struggle so hard upon their farms with the hope that the same tiling will be done for them that you are suggesting to-day should be done for the old soldier settlers, or a few of them who did not do so well upon their farms, possibly not through any fault of their own. I am not suggesting that for one second.
Thirdly, in your own province, sir, the legion last year at the provincial convention turned this proposal down cold in Saskatoon; and they, I think, are friends of the soldier settlers. For these reasons I think this committee should turn down the suggestion.
I was not at the Saskatoon convention. I do not know the officers of the legion in the Saskatoon area, but I happen to know personally some of the men who belong to that organization, and I feel quite satisfied that if they were given the true picture which we have given here from this side of the house and the other side of the picture from the government side, the men would be in a position to come to a fair decision. If that were done I am sure it would be entirely different from that given by the minister.
A little further down the minister had this to say:
Mr. Chairman, I should hate to intrude upon the discussion unduly, and I appreciate very strongly, as much as anyone in this committee, the sentimental appeal of those who have advocated this principle. But this principle will destroy the administration of the land settlement of veterans of the present war. I am convinced of that, and I am charged with a certain amount of responsibility in that. In the first place, there was a revaluation of the land prices mentioned by my friend, Mr. Wright. There was a revaluation time after time of the stock and equipment of the soldiers of the old war. The old soldier settlers are paying up to-day not only their actual debts but they are paying up by prepayments, hundreds of thousands of dollars, upon their settlement. There are only three hundred settlers in Canada who have asked for this concession, which means the destruction of a principle. I will not, as long as I am in charge of the administration, stand for the destruction of that principle; that is fair and clear.
I think that argument can be easily taken care of. On different occasions I have pointed out, particularly since the last war broke out, that much pressure has been brought to bear on the settlers. I also pointed out that the sons and daughters of many of these settlers have gone overseas and sent home part of their pay, and in some cases dependents^ allowances have been awarded to parents. In many cases children of the veteran settlers went to work in war factories and collected: good pay, and in order that their old folk might be protected in their declining years- and many of them have only a few to enjoy
Soldier Settlement

anyway-they sent home their money with which, along with all the pennies which the old folk could scrape together, the settlers have made these payments and prepayments. Many of us do not realize the anxiety facing these old people. Many of them are afraid of having the sheriff at the door. Quite a number of them have had that experience. They have had the experience of collectors coming around year after year, and in some cases the sheriff as well.
These people had money to spare because they were not able to buy machinery; they were not able to hire the help they needed; they could not buy materials which they should have had for their buildings. If one went around their farms and looked at their buildings, their homes, their farm equipment and their live stock he would see what I mean. I think he would agree that much of the money which has been paid in as advance payments, and which was advanced by the minister in his argument that clear titles should not be granted, should have been spent in building up the homes, farms and equipment of these old settlers.
The minister said that only three hundred settlers in Canada have asked for this concession. I pointed out last night that the petition was circulated, and I believe the minister obtained his figures from that petition. Incidentally I should like to know what it cost the soldier settlement board to get that information, to peruse the petition, to look over the names and find out who was asking for it. I wonder whether it did not cost more than $2,000 to obtain that information for the minister. We have not heard anything in the press about that. That may be worth while investigating in the Department of Veterans Affairs when they have the time to spare.
The petition was not circulated through all sections of the prairie provinces where most of these settlers are located. I pointed out that no pay was given to anybody; that those civilians and veterans carried the petition around over snow-blocked roads during the winter months and did not have the time thoroughly to cover the country. Had they had that time, I am quite satisfied there would have been a large number of settlers' names on the petition than the three hundred mentioned by the minister.
Later on, the minister said:
It is my duty to point out to the committee that the equity granted in varying ways at varying times to the old soldier settlers is $2,800 up to $4,000, and in some cases up to $6,000 instead of $2,320 under the present act.
If these amounts had been granted, then I say shame to any administration which

would stick any settler with debts of that kind, if it was necessary to make up the
S6.000	reduction.
It would appear that no opportunity was given to the committee to vote on whether or not clear titles would be granted, because we find the following at the bottom of page 1006:
Mr. Harris:	Mr. Chairman, there seems to
be a certain reluctance on the part of members present who have spoken in favour of this cancellation of the indebtedness to speak up at the moment.
If that remark did not appear I might have suggested that perhaps the members did not feel that they had full opportunity to vote; but Mr. Harris pleasantly took care of that for me. He went on to say:
My own views on the subject are well known. Therefore I move that this committee recommend that the period for applying for a writedown be extended to 1st September and that otherwise the committee take no action.
That had a negative effect on the motion. Before that amendment was carried a subamendment was moved by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), which reads as follows:
Mr. Wright: I wish to move a subamendment to the last amendment that the words "that otherwise no other action be taken" be struck out and that it read that an equity equal to that granted to the soldiers of the present war be granted to those applying for a write-down.
That subamendment was seconded by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch). When the vote was taken we find that the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Mutch) was the only member on the government side who voted in favour of the subamendment. However, because of the mustering of the reserves the motion was voted down. The recorded vote can be found on page IV of the minutes of proceedings of that day. I am not going to take the time and trouble to place on record the names of the members who voted for or against the subamendment as I have already placed on record the names of those who attended the meeting, and all government members except the hon. member for Winnipeg south voted against.
May I now deal with the request of the delegation of the soldier settlers? These men left here on May 7 with the expectation of having some favourable word sent to them either by wire or by air mail that something worth while was being done. I know they felt disappointed when the result of the committee's vote was transmitted to them. Personally I am disappointed and I believe that many hon. members, including members on the government side of the house, are also disappointed.

Soldier Settlement
For some time I have had a resolution on the order paper, and I may say that at the next session I intend to place on the order paper another resolution which will have the same effect. I had intended to place this resolution back on the order paper, but because it contains certain statements which perhaps are not agreeable to the government T am not permitted to do so. However, I shall have another one prepared which will have the same effect. The resolution which I had on the order paper reads as follows:
Whereas veterans of great war I who settled on land under the soldier settlement scheme as well as their wives and families, have in many instances suffered severe hardships because of purchase of land, live stock and equipment at inflationary prices, and low prices received for farm products brought about by lack of adequate policy for agriculture;
And whereas we are now embarking on another land scheme for veterans of the present war, under a government policy that does not guarantee cost of production, the success of which scheme may be jeopardized by the apparent failure of the former soldier settlement board scheme.
Therefore be it resolved,-that, in the opinion ot this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of giving clear titles to all soldier settlers who on March 31, 1944, held land under contract with the soldier settlement board.
This resolution was discussed on October 1, last, the first time we had a private members' day since the outbreak of the war. By means of a prolonged argument, including family allowances and other matters, the debate on the resolution continued until eleven o'clock and then it was sent to the committee. I am disappointed in the findings of that committee.
In conclusion, I wish to say that I, and the old veterans, do not ask for one cent of charity. I believe Canada owes those men a debt of gratitude as well as a square deal in connection with the land, live stock and equipment they have bought. They have asked for simple justice, nothing more and nothing less, and I believe they are entitled to it. Simple justice should be placed before monetary values or anything of that kind. There were 25,017 settlers placed on the land, and the average credit extended was $4,358.40. As of March 31, 1944, some 6,153 settlers, or 25 per cent of the original number, were still on the land with an average debt of $1,254, which represented 29 per cent of the average loan, after twenty-five years of heart-breaking work which would not have been necessary if a proper economic system had been organized and the affairs of the country properly managed. After twenty-five years some 4,130 settlers, or 16 per cent, have secured title. That is quite a record. The rate of interest of five per cent on current account and seven per cent on
arrears should never have been charged anyone in this country. If we would only take the trouble to study the source of money and the backing of money I think we would agree that these things should not be allowed. Some day sooner or later, perhaps too late, this will have to be changed.
Under the Veterans Land Act the maximum loan available for full-time farming is $6,000 at 3| per cent. Here again, I believe the rate of interest is too high, particularly when we consider the fact that only a short time ago we made a loan to Great Britain on which no interest is to be paid until 1951, after which the interest is at the rate of only two per cent. Do we owe our own men as much as we owe Great Britain? I am not opposed to the loan to Great Britain, but I say we should extend to our own war veterans the same rate or an even better rate. Again, many of the men coming under the Veterans Land Act are sons of veterans of the first great war. Why should they receive preferred treatment? Why should the old veterans not receive treatment as good as that being given their sons at the . present time? If a settler takes full advantage of the credit extended under the Veterans Land Act he may get a clear grant of $2,320 on certain conditions, which is equal to 39 per cent of the total credit extended. At the end of March, 1944, the average debt of the old settlers was 29 per cent of the original amount. I do not think we are asking anything out of the way when we ask that this be wiped out. These men are all Canadians.
I am not dealing with them as Liberals or Conservatives or supporters of any political party. I am dealing with them as Canadians, men who went overseas to save Canada.
Some of these men failed because they were entirely unsuited to farm life. They paid far too much for their land, live stock and implements. In some cases they were given land in dry or frost areas. At the time they bought their land prices of agricultural products were high. They paid high prices for the land and implements, which in many cases deteriorated until they were worth only ten per cent of what they cost when the deals were made. It has been admitted by the former minister of mines and resources that this was a hastily improvised scheme. From the information we have obtained and from the results we have seen, I do not think we could disagree with that statement by Hon. T. A. Crerar. It was intended as a rehabilitation measure, but actually it turned out to be a way of persecuting our old soldiers. At present the average age of the settlers is nearly sixty, and we find some still operating at eighty years of age and over. Take any
Soldier Settlement

member of this or the other house sixty or seventy years of age; put him on a poor farm, with poor equipment, with some debt to carry and an uncertain market for his products. He will find out just how he feels about it. I think we can use our imagination a little along that line. If these men could not pay off their debts in twenty-five years, covering the prime of their lives, how can we expect them to pay up now? Again let us use our imagination. Some of these old fellows will be over a hundred years old by the time the twenty-year extension of their contracts will expire, and I do not think we are going to have very many of them around at that time. As I have pointed out already, they are in need of better homes, better buildings, better equipment and some of the comforts of life, as well as medical and dental care.
As I pointed out earlier, the treatment we are giving the old veterans will have a detrimental effect on the settling of young men under the Veterans Land Act, because any man who sees his father threatened with eviction will wonder whether he should undertake a contract and also run the risk of being kicked out on the road after a certain time. Again-and this is a point I brought up on another occasion-we sold land to the old soldier settlers at values based upon prices of farm products at that time. When those contracts were made no clause was written into them providing that prices of farm products would remain at that level until these debts were paid off. This is one reason why the present Veterans Land Act may also fail; and when the proper time comes to discuss that matter I am going to suggest again that a clause be written into the contracts guaranteeing these men the same prices for the products they raise, whatever they may be-wheat, live stock or whatever it is-until the contracts are cleared up. The settler is bound by contract, and I think the government should be bound in exactly the same manner. Surely that is not asking too much.
There is one more reason why we might claim this write-off, or adjustment or settlement, call it w'hat you will as long as we get the result. Only yesterday we were told that a million dollars or more would be written off homes now being built for veterans of the last war, even before they have moved in. That is one more argument to support our claim. The cost of collection has been given as $100,000 a year. I should like to see audited figures bearing out that statement, because I do not believe it is correct. If it is accurate, why did it cost an average of $1,100,000 a year during the first twenty-five

years this scheme was in operation? Where did the waste come in, and where is it coming in at the present time?
We believe the resolution on the order paper at the present time precedes a bill that will be final as far as the old settlers are concerned. We are not satisfied with it, I do not think many hon. members on the government side are satisfied1 with it, and I am sure all the members of the opposition are dissatisfied. As I suggested in beginning my presentation yesterday, I should like to see this resolution withdrawn and another brought forward preceding a bill that would give clear title to all the old settlers who had contracts with the board at the end of March, 1944. I am sure that would receive the unanimous support of the house. If there is some influence outside parliament opposing this, I think we should be able to dispose of it. In my opinion we owe a debt of gratitude to the men with whom we are dealing at the present time. The government should certainly see to it that the promise made by the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden in 1917 to the Canadian expeditionary force should not be dishonoured, even though this government is not of the same political stripe as was that right hon. gentleman.

I do not propose to hold up matters this afternoon; but, following the debate, one might be led to believe that this hardship was experienced only in western Canada. I wish to dispel that thought, because I know of many cases in Ontario. I have one in mind particularly respecting a young man who was buying a piece of property for $2,800, but who fell behind in his payments, with the result that a quit-claim was executed. Later, that land was sold by the department to a private individual for $1,400, just half the amount the veteran was supposed to have paid for it.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr Mackenzie thereupon moved for leave to introduce bill No. 199, to amend the Soldier Settlement Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first
time.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.

speechtext:
Mr. W. A. TUCKER (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to provide that the members of the women's royal naval services and the South African military

Veterans Affairs-Women's Services
nursing service shall be entitled to the rights, privileges and benefits enjoyed by Canadians serving in His Majesty's forces other than Canadian forces during world war II under the Veterans Land Act, 1942, the Veterans Insurance Act, the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946, the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, 1942, the Civil Service Act, the Pension Act, the Income War Tax Act, the Department of Veterans Affairs Act and the War Service Grants Act.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: Would the parliamentary assistant give an explanation?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this measure is something with which I am sure all hon. members will be in agreement. It was found that Canadian girls who went into the women's royal naval services actually had not the same rights as if they had gone into the branch of the air service in Great Britain, or the branch of the army. By some ruling of British law the women's royal naval services were not actually part of the military forces of Great Britain, and for that reason they did not get the benefit of the act which conferred rights on Canadians who went into His Majesty's forces, other than Canadian forces.
The purpose of this measure is to give to Canadian girls who were domiciled in Canada at the time they entered the women's royal naval services the same rights as if they had gone into a similar branch of the army or air force, namely all the rights of anyone who went into His Majesty's forces, other than Canadian. Those rights are set out in the resolution. Any rights which are given to them by British law will be supplemented up to the level they would have had, had they been in the Canadian forces. That is set out in the resolution as rights which they will have under the Veterans Land Act, 1942, the Veterans Insurance Act, the Veterans Rehabilitation Act, the War Veterans Allowance Act, 1946, the Reinstatement in Civil Employment Act, 1942, the Civil Service Act, the Pension Act, the Income War Tax Act, the Department of Veterans Affairs Act and the War Service Grants Act.
The same is true in regard to Canadian girls who went into the South African military nursing service. It was found that under South African law they were not members of His Majesty's forces of South Africa; so that they did not get the benefit of our legislation which conferred these rights on those who went into His Majesty's forces, other than Canadian forces.
The purpose of this bill is to give Canadian girls domiciled in Canada, who went into the South African military nursing service, or who went into the women's royal naval services the
same rights as if they had gone into an actual branch of His Majesty's forces, other than Canadian forces. It will put them in that position. The matter has already been covered by order in council, so far as the South African military nursing service is concerned. It was passed after a resolution recommending it by the veterans committee of the house.
The provision respecting the women's royal naval services has not been brought into effect, and will become effective only after this bill has been passed by parliament, and becomes law.
Might I emphasize that the order in council respecting the South African military service requires domicile and residence in Canada at the time of going into this service. The bill will require only domicile at the time of entering the service. In order to get the rights they must have domicile and residence at the time of applying for these rights. In other words, they must come back to Canada.
The only other matter which perhaps I should mention would have reference to Canadian girls who went into the voluntary aid detachment, who served in Red Cross work overseas or who served in the St. John Ambulance Corps overseas. The problem of what should be done in connection with these people was referred by our committee to a subcommittee of that committee. A study is being made, and the recommendation by the subcommittee will be considered shortly, I hope, by the main committee, at least when an opportunity presents itself. I can say, too, that the matter is receiving the active study of the government. It has not been overlooked, but is a matter the solution of which requires some time.
I hope that this bill which gives these rights to Canadian girls will meet with such unanimity of support that perhaps we might advance the measure some considerable distance this afternoon.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with what has been said by the parliamentary assistant, namely that this bill simply carries out a matter of justice to these two branches of the services, namely the Wrens and the South African nurses.
It does not concern very many people; I believe there were only about fifty Wrens concerned, and about 298 South African nurses. Had it not been for a technicality, both the Wrens and the nurses would have been members of His Majesty's forces. The South African nurses were recruited in Canada at the request of the Canadian government and sent to South Africa to assist our sister dominion. The report from South Africa is

Veterans Affairs-Women's Services
that they did splendid work, and there is no reason why they should not be treated the same as nursing sisters who served in other parts of the world.
There is one matter I should like to raise in connection with the Pension Act. I should like to know if it is intended to amend this act in order to extend the insurance principle to the South African nurses? Perhaps the parliamentary assistant can give me my answer later on. I brought up this matter in the committee and at that time the minister said that he thought it would be looked after. However, we did not have a definite answer. There was also considerable anxiety among committee members as to whether the Red Cross, the V.A.D., the St. John Ambulance Corps, the merchant marine, the firefighters, the auxiliary services and others would receive consideration. The committee did not feel like recommending this bill until they had some assurance that these other people would be looked after. As the parliamentary assistant has said, bills are being prepared to cover the firefighters and, I believe, the auxiliary services, while the V.A.D., the Red Cross, the St. John Ambulance Corps, the merchant marine and others are being considered by a subcommittee of the veterans affairs committee and we have the assurance of the minister that their cases will be given every consideration.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
That being the case, we are in accord with this bill which will follow this resolution now being presented by the parliamentary assistant.
Mr. D. K. HAZE.N (St. John-Albert): Mr. Speaker, I should like to inquire about Canadian nurses who enlisted for service in South Africa. Some of these nurses have complained to me that they did not receive the remuneration they were told they would receive when they enlisted for service in South Africa. After they had entered into the agreement, and even while some of them were on the boat, they were told that while they would receive the amount they were told they would receive, it would be subject to certain deductions. The hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) has said that these nurses were recruited by the Canadian government.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: That is not accurate. These nurses were not recruited by the Canadian government; they were recruited by the South African government, and the Department of National Defence acted as agent for the South African government in presenting the conditions of service and in arranging for the enlistment of these young ladies.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: Indirectly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: It was not indirectly. The Canadian government did not recruit them and their enlistment was neither at the desire nor request of nor on conditions laid down by the Canadian government.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: I understand from the minister that the Canadian government acted as agent for the South African government?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: To put it mildly, there was a misunderstanding about the matter and these Canadian nurses did not receive the payments that they understood they would receive. It seems to me that as a matter of equity they are entitled to receive what the South African government agreed to pay them and what they expected to receive. No doubt some of these complaints have come to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs and I should like to ask his parliamentary assistant if they are being considered and if the bill that is to be brought in will remedy what these people think is an injustice.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
I would call the attention of hon. members to the rules which state that the proper place to ask questions of the parliamentary assistant is in committee.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
If no legislation is to be brought down this session to take care of the Red Cross workers, then I want to impress upon the committee the importance of giving consideration to these people. The question of Red Cross nurses was brought up last fall, and I brought it up in the committee on veterans affairs on April 5. This resolution was introduced on April 12. The hon. member for Vancouver North followed me and he tried to impress upon the committee the importance of giving consideration to the members of the St. John Ambulance Corps.
I do not think this resolution goes far enough. Will these people be considered this session? I would emphasize the fact that these girls signed attestation papers and they were discharged in the regular way. Girls who attended universities and schools last fall and finished the term are being denied the recognition that is given to others.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Royal asked whether girls who entered the South African nursing service would have the benefit of the insurance principle. I think everybody in the committee wanted them to have that benefit, but the question that arises in connection with this

Veterans Affairs-Women's Services
matter can be placed quite easily before this committee. The purpose of this legislation is to bring the benefits up to a level of those given to people who served in the Canadian forces. For example, a person who served in the forces of the United Kingdom would, if his entitlement were approved by the United Kingdom, have his pension rights brought up to the same level as though he had served in the Canadian forces. In the first instance, because the service documents and everything else that has to do with the matter are in the possession of the United Kingdom government, the matter is left to them for a ruling whether there is entitlement or not. After they have made a ruling for entitlement, we supplement the payments. It has been brought home to us that the system has worked satisfactorily. Since the first great war there has been great harmony and cooperation between the representative of the British pension ministry in Canada and our own pension commission. They point out that that is probably the only way to handle it, because the British pension people have to rule on entitlement in the first place.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: This has to do with South Africa.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
I am coming to that. If the British authorities gave a ruling which did not satisfy the applicant and a separate application to the commission was possible, our pension commission would become a sort of appeal board from the British pension authorities. They say that if we do not follow the same principle in regard to the South African nursing service, namely, leave it in the first place to South Africa for a ruling, the same difficulties will arise. They further point out that if we did not leave it in the first instance for a ruling by the South African authorities we would be introducing a precedent that might cause difficulty in carrying on as satisfactorily as we have done in connection with those who served in the United Kingdom forces. The matter can be further discussed in committee on the civilian pensions bill. I must say that it looked to me as if it would be a difficult thing to do otherwise than as suggested. However, the door is not closed. But it is a matter of difficulty.
The hon. member for St. John-Albert brought up the question of the benefits the South African nurses expected to have received while serving. Of course this bill deals with them only at and after their discharge, so that I hope he will not mind if I suggest to him that he direct his shafts in some other direction.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: I was asking if it had been brought to the attention of your department.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
It may have been. There are so many things come in that I would not want to say that it has not, but I have not it very clearly in my mind that it has. At any rate, if it did come in, I would pass it on probably to the Department of National Defence.
In regard to what the hon. member for Kingston City has mentioned, I can only repeat to him what I said at the start. The veterans affairs committee has still eleven bills to consider. It has a very heavy task ahead of it. For that reason we referred the question of the Red Cross nurses, the V.A.D.'s and the St. John Ambulance workers and other people who were not actually in the armed services, including the fire fighters and supervisors to a subcommittee of our committee for study. They are studying it and are, I understand, on the verge of making a report. I think I can say to him, and he will bear me out in this, that the committee will try to get through all the work it possibly can before prorogation. That is all I can say about the matter. The order in which the work will be taken will be decided by the committee itself. If we can get through all the work we shall certainly make some recommendation in regard to these Red Cross nurses, V.A.D's and St. John Ambulance people. It is just a matter of what we can physically do. If we can possibly do it, I can assure him that the committee will consider the matter and make a recommendation.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: I hope the parliamentary assistant will realize that there is a hardship on these nurses who have attended schools and universities on the understanding that they will be granted the same conditions. The fall term is coming along and they have to pay their own fees. I hope the minister realizes the seriousness and importance of the matter to these girls.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: Everyone seems to be in favour of the principle. May I ask how many girls are involved?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext: There is no certainty as to the exact figures, but I think there are approximately 300 in the South African nurses group and from fifty to sixty in the women's royal naval services group.

subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think the lack of debate reveals general agreement on this resolution. I would point out, however, that it includes only the women's royal naval services and the South African military nursing service. It has been intimated that later on



Veterans Affairs-Women's Services
other groups will be brought in. There is already on the order paper a resolution to bring in a bill for the benefit of the fire fighters, but the acts under which these groups are going to benefit are not set out on the order paper. Will there be some difference between the treatment of the firefighters and these other auxiliary services?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: ENTITLEMENT OF CERTAIN WOMEN'S SERVICES TO REHABILITATION BENEFITS, ETC.
speechtext:
The committee made a recommendation in regard to the firefighters and supervisors. Then the government decided to introduce legislation in regard to these two groups. Various members of the committee then pointed out that in their opinion the nurses who served in the Red Cross and in the St. John Ambulance Association were just as much entitled to consideration as the firefighters and supervisors, and that if we went ahead with legislation for the firefighters and supervisors it would lead to a debate as to why these other groups should not be included. So that the whole matter was referred to a special committee for study and report to the main committee. The understanding was that in the meantime, until a decision was arrived at in the light of the report of the subcommittee by our main committee, the government would not proceed with its bill for the firefighters and supervisors. That is why they are not being proceeded with although they are on the order paper for the resolution stage of course.
Resolution reported, read the second time and concurred in. Mr. Tucker thereupon moved for leave to introduce bill No. 200, respecting benefits for those serving in the women's royal naval services and the South African military nursing service.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

The house resumed from Monday, May 20, consideration in committee of bill No. 57, to amend the Royal Canadian Air Force Act- Mr. Gibson (Hamilton West)-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 1-Short title.

speakeroldname: Hon. COLIN GIBSON (Minister of National Defence for Air):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: This bill was considered on May 20 and a good deal of discussion took place on that occasion. Since that time, a similar bill has been passed to provide for the naval cadets, and this contains much the same provisions in relation to the Royal Canadian Air Force. It is a very similar measure, providing for air cadets, and I hope that it will be possible to get it through to-day. [Mr. Castleden.3
Will the ages be the same as in the bill introduced by the minister's colleague?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: The age limit is from fifteen to eighteen inclusive.
I believe the other was from sixteen to nineteen.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: From twelve to nineteen.

I wish to ask the minister one or two questions. The first has to do with the administration or direction of air cadets. I understand that the sea cadets are directed almost entirely by the sea cadet league and supervised by the naval service, but that the air cadets are directed to a large extent by the R.C.A.F.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I was not paying attention. Did I understand the hon. member to be addressing his remarks to me? If so, will he repeat what he said as to the manner of handling sea cadets.

I was speaking of the direction of the sea cadet movement, I believe the navy league have greater power and authority than the air cadet league. From my own knowledge of the subject, I believe this to be the case. I feel that if the air cadets are to progress, as we all want them to progress, and to be a strong and thriving body in peace as they were in war, they are faced with a problem of direction that calls for solution. I refer particularly to the dual authority from which they have suffered during the war years, one authority originating in the service with air cadet league liaison officers and the second authority originating with the provincial governments and their departments of education, which should have a certain amount of jurisdiction over air cadets in school squadrons. I would ask the minister to define for us the powers of the service, the R.C.A.F., the air cadet league and the provincial departments of education with regard to the cadet squadrons we propose to continue in peace.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
The distribution of authority as between the R.C.A.F. and the air cadet league was set out in the various letters written by the Minister of National Defence for Air in 1942, dealing with the division of authority between the two bodies. The Minister of National Defence for Air approves the formation of air cadet units, prescribes qualifications as to medical fitness, and appoints such persons as may be necessary or desirable to commissions in the Royal Canadian Air Force for the purpose of serving as air cadet instructors. He prescribes the terms and conditions under which air cadets may be

Royal Canadian Air Force
provided uniforms, provides for medical care and hospitalization for air cadets undergoing training at camps, prescribes a course of training for air cadets and for instructors and officers.
The league is responsible for maintaining headquarters at Ottawa to assist the air force and encourage, by publicity and other means, the formation of air cadet units, subject to the concurrence of the minister, and makes such recommendations of suitable persons to serve as officers in the units and for appointment to His Majesty's commission, also as to promotions or retirements, and to enrol as air cadets such lads as are desirable for the units which have alreads^ been authorized. The air cadet league also looks after the award of trophies, badges and other awards considered suitable, and administers all funds received by the league.
What provision is made for uniforms and for equipment for the air cadet squadrons?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: Up to the present the cadet squadrons have received a clothing allowance and also maintenance allowance of $1.25 a year to maintain uniforms. Consideration is being given at the present time, in negotiations with the league, for changing that provision and having the uniforms provided by the R.C.A.F., the units to be responsible for maintaining them.

I have no desire to hold up the passage of this measure, but I thought we should hear from the minister regarding one or two points and perhaps the committee might sit a few minutes after six o'clock. I wish to repeat my question because I feel that the very survival of the air cadet corps depends on the manner of direction, and if authority is to be divided between the R.C.A.F. the air cadet league and the provincial departments of education there is this difficulty, that they have to agree with everybody and there will be confusion. There will be no singleness of command. I suggest that a clear chain of command is most essential to the survival of the air cadet league and the squadrons in the way in which we wish them to continue.
I would also put to the minister a question which I asked the Minister of National Defence. That question was: Is the interservice cadet committee considering standardization of pay and allowances and uniform conditions of service and commission for all three cadet corps, or are they all handling their own organizations and conducting them by different- means?
63260-182^	.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: At present they are all operating separately under the guidance of the three defence departments, but the inter-service cadet committee was asked recently to make recommendations as to the conditions of service and regulations applying to the various cadet corps so as to provide as far as possible for the same treatment as between the army cadets, the navy cadets and the air force cadets, but all will receive approximately the same support as far as that can be arranged.

I attended the annual meeting of the navy league which was held some time ago, and the matter was mentioned up there. I have forgotten what was said on that occasion. I have a friendly feeling for the proposed air cadet corps, but my memory is-and I am not clear on just what was said-that there should be no rivalry between the sea cadets and the air cadets. Is the minister able to tell us the number of air cadets in Toronto and at other similar points? Without passing judgment on this matter, because I have nothing tangible in front of me, will there be any conflict in the method of organization of the air brigade or corps, or whatever it may be called? Will there be a voluntary band of men and women behind this organization, such as is behind the navy league?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext:
It is
already in being; this is not new. The air cadets were formed in 1940, but they were operating under the War Measures Act. It is now necessary to provide a bill in order that their future may be assured. At the present time the air cadets have about 289 squadrons throughout Canada. They plan to maintain a strength of about 15,000 air cadets in time of peace. That is about the same number as the navy has under contemplation.

I am not going to oppose this bill, because I realize that a development along this line would likely have the same beneficial effect on the young people as the navy league has had. It would train them to love the air service, to be young gentlemen, to be civil and courteous, to be active and to attain the other characteristics which go with the training in any well organized youth organization.

Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
